text: Scientists cracked open a rock from the bottom of the ocean... and found two hundred forty-five animals living inside.
And mining companies want to scoop up billions of these rocks.
They're called nodules. Potato-sized lumps on the Pacific floor, up to four miles down.
They grow so slowly, one can take millions of years to form.
Researchers examined two hundred forty-four of them. Inside, they counted over four thousand tiny animals.
One single nodule held two hundred forty-five. A whole hidden city... in one rock.
And these animals weren't the same as the ones living in the mud around them.
Why does that matter? Because these rocks are packed with metals for batteries.
The U.S. could certify its first commercial deep-sea mining permit as soon as December.
Which means some of these tiny worlds could be scooped up... before we even know what lives there.
Should we mine the deep sea for batteries?
